messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 44
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Nurse
- Trauma Type: Mugging or robbery
- Pcl5: 68

# The Weight of an Ordinary Evening

Rajan is a 44-year-old Filipino man who has spent nearly two decades as a registered nurse in a busy urban hospital. His colleagues describe him as steady, unflappable — the kind of person you want beside you when a patient codes at three in the morning. He has held that reputation carefully, built it year by year, and it matters deeply to him.

Fourteen months ago, on a Tuesday evening in late autumn, Rajan was walking from the hospital parking structure to a nearby pharmacy to pick up his wife's prescription. It was just past seven o'clock, still light enough that he felt no particular caution. Two men approached him from a doorway. One pressed something hard into his ribs — he still doesn't know whether it was a gun or a pipe — and told him not to move. They took his wallet, his watch, and his phone. The whole encounter lasted perhaps ninety seconds. Then they were gone, and Rajan was standing alone on the sidewalk, his hands shaking so badly he couldn't button his jacket.

He drove himself home. He told his wife, Marisol, that he'd been robbed, accepted her embrace, and then went to shower. Under the water, he began trembling again, a full-body shaking he couldn't control, and he stayed there until the hot water ran out. He told himself it was over. He told himself he was fine.

He was not fine.

Within two weeks, Rajan stopped taking the route past that pharmacy entirely, adding fifteen minutes to his commute without explanation. He began parking as close to the hospital entrance as possible, sometimes arriving an hour early simply to secure a spot near the door. At work, he notices himself scanning the faces of visitors who enter the unit — cataloguing them, measuring them against some internal threat assessment he can't turn off. When a family member raised his voice at the nurses' station last spring, Rajan froze completely for several seconds, his body convinced, in that moment, that something terrible was beginning again.

Sleep has become its own ordeal. He lies awake most nights replaying the ninety seconds on that sidewalk, but the memory has grown distorted — in the version that visits him at two in the morning, the men don't leave. He wakes from these dreams rigid, heart hammering, and then lies still so he won't disturb Marisol, staring at the ceiling until his alarm sounds. He is exhausted in a way that rest no longer touches.

What troubles Rajan most, and what he speaks about with the most difficulty, is what has happened to his sense of himself at work. He has always drawn a quiet pride from his composure — from the fact that he could be present with suffering without being consumed by it. Now he finds himself emotionally blunted during shifts, going through procedures with technical precision while feeling strangely absent from his own hands. He documents everything correctly. He says the right things to patients and families. But he describes it as performing a role he used to simply inhabit. A patient's adult son wept at the bedside last month, and Rajan felt nothing, and that frightened him more than the weeping would have.

He has told almost no one. He mentioned it once to a colleague who responded with something like, *at least you weren't hurt*, and Rajan nodded and changed the subject. He has not told his supervisor. He worries that admitting vulnerability will cost him the professional identity he has spent so long constructing, that the steadiness his colleagues trust in him will be revealed as something he no longer actually possesses.

Marisol has noticed the distance. She asks careful questions he deflects with careful answers. On weekends, he rarely leaves the house unless necessary. He gardens, methodically, in the small backyard — pulling weeds, turning soil — and describes it as the only time his mind goes quiet, the only hour in the day when his body feels like it belongs to him again.
